claim: Multiple spaced trials of aversive differential conditioning can produce two independent long-term memories (LTMs) of opposite valence in Drosophila.
source: Multiple spaced trials of aversive differential conditioning can produce two independent long-term memories (LTMs) of opposite valence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established findings in the field.

claim: One memory from multiple spaced trials is an aversive memory for avoiding the conditioned stimulus (CS+).
source: One is an aversive memory for avoiding the conditioned stimulus (CS+), and the other is a safety memory for approaching the non-conditioned stimulus (CS–).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the literature on differential conditioning.

claim: One memory from multiple spaced trials is a safety memory for approaching the non-conditioned stimulus (CS–).
source: One is an aversive memory for avoiding the conditioned stimulus (CS+), and the other is a safety memory for approaching the non-conditioned stimulus (CS–).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the literature on differential conditioning.

claim: A single trial of aversive differential conditioning yields one merged LTM (mLTM) for avoiding both CS+ and CS–.
source: Here, we show that a single trial of aversive differential conditioning yields one merged LTM (mLTM) for avoiding both CS+ and CS–.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The merged LTM can be detected after sequential exposures to the shock-paired CS+ and -unpaired CS–.
source: Such mLTM can be detected after sequential exposures to the shock-paired CS+ and -unpaired CS–, and be retrieved by either CS+ or CS–.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and results shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The merged LTM can be retrieved by either CS+ or CS–.
source: Such mLTM can be detected after sequential exposures to the shock-paired CS+ and -unpaired CS–, and be retrieved by either CS+ or CS–.
evidence: This is supported by the extinction experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The formation of mLTM relies on triggering aversive-reinforcing dopaminergic neurons.
source: The formation of mLTM relies on triggering aversive-reinforcing dopaminergic neurons and subsequent new protein synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by the neural manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The formation of mLTM relies on new protein synthesis.
source: The formation of mLTM relies on triggering aversive-reinforcing dopaminergic neurons and subsequent new protein synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by the cycloheximide treatment experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expressing mLTM involves αβ Kenyon cells.
source: Expressing mLTM involves αβ Kenyon cells and corresponding approach-directing mushroom body output neurons, in which similar-amplitude long-term depression of responses to CS+ and CS– seems to signal the mLTM.
evidence: This is supported by the neural manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expressing mLTM involves approach-directing mushroom body output neurons.
source: Expressing mLTM involves αβ Kenyon cells and corresponding approach-directing mushroom body output neurons, in which similar-amplitude long-term depression of responses to CS+ and CS– seems to signal the mLTM.
evidence: This is supported by the neural manipulation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Similar-amplitude long-term depression of responses to CS+ and CS– in mushroom body output neurons signals the mLTM.
source: Expressing mLTM involves αβ Kenyon cells and corresponding approach-directing mushroom body output neurons, in which similar-amplitude long-term depression of responses to CS+ and CS– seems to signal the mLTM.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Animals can develop distinct strategies for occasional and repeated threatening experiences.
source: Our results suggest that animals can develop distinct strategies for occasional and repeated threatening experiences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of single-trial and multi-trial conditioning results.

claim: Aversive differential conditioning is widely used to study memories produced by threatening experiences from invertebrates to humans.
source: From invertebrates to humans, aversive differential conditioning is widely used to study memories produced by threatening experiences (Carew et al., 1983; Corches et al., 2019; Gentile et al., 1986; Schneider et al., 1999; Tully and Quinn, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: After repetitive spaced trials of conditioning, animals form two complementary long-term memories (LTMs) of opposite valence.
source: After repetitive spaced trials of conditioning, animals form two complementary long-term memories (LTMs) of opposite valence (Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Pollak et al., 2008; Pollak et al., 2010), including the aversive memory to the conditioned stimulus (CS+) and the rewarding memory to the non-conditioned stimulus (CS–) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Complementary LTMs result in enhanced long-lasting discrimination between CS+ and CS– through guiding avoidance to CS+ and approach to CS–.
source: Such complementary LTMs result in enhanced long-lasting discrimination between CS+ and CS– through guiding avoidance to CS+ and approach to CS–.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of complementary LTMs.

claim: It remains unclear whether and how occasional threatening experiences would induce long-lasting changes in future escape behavior.
source: However, it remains unclear whether and how occasional threatening experiences, such as single-trial conditionings, would induce long-lasting changes in future escape behavior.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Experience-dependent long-lasting behavioral modifications mainly rely on the formation of LTMs from invertebrates to humans.
source: From invertebrates to humans, experience-dependent long-lasting behavioral modifications mainly rely on the formation of LTMs (Kandel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established knowledge.

claim: In Drosophila, there are at least two categories of aversive olfactory LTMs that last for more than 7 days.
source: In Drosophila, there are at least two categories of aversive olfactory LTMs that last for more than 7 days.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila memory.

claim: Spaced training-induced LTM can be observed after repetitive spaced training with inter-trial rests.
source: One is the spaced training-induced LTM that can be observed after repetitive spaced training with inter-trial rests (multiple trials with a 15 min rest interval between each), but not after either single-trial training or repetitive massed training without interval (Tully et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Spaced training-induced LTM cannot be observed after single-trial training.
source: One is the spaced training-induced LTM that can be observed after repetitive spaced training with inter-trial rests (multiple trials with a 15 min rest interval between each), but not after either single-trial training or repetitive massed training without interval (Tully et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Spaced training-induced LTM cannot be observed after repetitive massed training without interval.
source: One is the spaced training-induced LTM that can be observed after repetitive spaced training with inter-trial rests (multiple trials with a 15 min rest interval between each), but not after either single-trial training or repetitive massed training without interval (Tully et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Forming spaced training-induced aversive LTM requires new protein synthesis.
source: Forming such aversive LTM requires new protein synthesis and the paired posterior lateral 1 (PPL1) cluster of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) to depress the connection between odor-activated Kenyon cells (KCs) in the mushroom body (MB) αβ lobe and downstream α2sc (MB-V2) MB output neurons (MBONs) (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Cognigni et al., 2018; Modi et al., 2020; Pascual and Préat, 2001; Plaçais et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Forming spaced training-induced aversive LTM requires the paired posterior lateral 1 (PPL1) cluster of dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
source: Forming such aversive LTM requires new protein synthesis and the paired posterior lateral 1 (PPL1) cluster of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) to depress the connection between odor-activated Kenyon cells (KCs) in the mushroom body (MB) αβ lobe and downstream α2sc (MB-V2) MB output neurons (MBONs) (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Cognigni et al., 2018; Modi et al., 2020; Pascual and Préat, 2001; Plaçais et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Forming spaced training-induced aversive LTM requires depression of the connection between odor-activated Kenyon cells (KCs) in the mushroom body (MB) αβ lobe and downstream α2sc (MB-V2) MB output neurons (MBONs).
source: Forming such aversive LTM requires new protein synthesis and the paired posterior lateral 1 (PPL1) cluster of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) to depress the connection between odor-activated Kenyon cells (KCs) in the mushroom body (MB) αβ lobe and downstream α2sc (MB-V2) MB output neurons (MBONs) (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Cognigni et al., 2018; Modi et al., 2020; Pascual and Préat, 2001; Plaçais et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Context-dependent LTM forms after single-trial training and does not require protein synthesis-dependent consolidation.
source: The other is a recently reported context-dependent LTM that forms after single-trial training, which does not require protein synthesis-dependent consolidation (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The expression of context-dependent LTM relies on multisensory integration in the lateral horn.
source: The expression of context-dependent LTM relies on multisensory integration in the lateral horn and is not affected by blocking KCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Zhao et al., 2019).

claim: Context-dependent LTM is not affected by blocking KCs.
source: The expression of context-dependent LTM relies on multisensory integration in the lateral horn and is not affected by blocking KCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Zhao et al., 2019).

claim: Memory performance evaluation has been based on testing the discrimination between CS+ and CS–.
source: However, all these observations derived from the same design principle that evaluates memory performance through testing the discrimination between CS+ and CS– (Tully and Quinn, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Direct responses to CS+ and CS– have been largely overlooked in prior studies.
source: Thus, direct responses to CS+ and CS– have been largely overlooked.
evidence: This is an inference based on the focus of prior studies on discrimination.

claim: A third-odor test was introduced in which flies were given a choice between either CS+ and a novel odor, or CS– and a novel odor.
source: In the current study, we introduced a third-odor test, in which flies were given a choice between either CS+ and a novel odor, or CS– and a novel odor.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Single-trial differential conditioning produces a merged LTM (mLTM) guiding avoidances of both CS+ and CS– for several days after training.
source: We therefore identified that the single-trial differential conditioning produces a merged LTM (mLTM) guiding avoidances of both CS+ and CS– for several days after training.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by behavioral experiments.

claim: The encoding of mLTM involves new protein synthesis.
source: The encoding and expression of such mLTM involve new protein synthesis, PPL1 DANs, αβ KCs, and α2sc MBONs.
evidence: This is supported by the cycloheximide treatment experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The encoding of mLTM involves PPL1 DANs.
source: The encoding and expression of such mLTM involve new protein synthesis, PPL1 DANs, αβ KCs, and α2sc MBONs.

claim: The expression of mLTM involves αβ KCs.
source: The encoding and expression of such mLTM involve new protein synthesis, PPL1 DANs, αβ KCs, and α2sc MBONs.
evidence: This is supported by the neural manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression of mLTM involves α2sc MBONs.
source: The encoding and expression of such mLTM involve new protein synthesis, PPL1 DANs, αβ KCs, and α2sc MBONs.
evidence: This is supported by the neural manipulation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Animals utilize distinct escape strategies for facing occasional and repeated dangers.
source: These findings suggest that animals utilize distinct escape strategies for facing occasional and repeated dangers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of single-trial and multi-trial conditioning results.

claim: Flies exposed to single-trial conditioning rapidly lost their ability to discriminate CS+ and CS– within 1 day.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Davis and Zhong, 2017; Shuai et al., 2010; Tully et al., 1994), flies exposed to single-trial conditioning rapidly lost their ability to discriminate CS+ and CS– within 1 day.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior work.

claim: Trained flies gradually exhibited significant avoidances of both CS+ and CS– from 12 hr to more than 7 days after training when tested against a novel odor.
source: However, when trained flies were instead tested between either CS+ and a novel odor, or CS– and a novel odor, they gradually exhibited significant avoidances of both CS+ and CS– from 12 hr to more than 7 days after training (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Testing CS+ or CS– versus air revealed training-induced long-lasting avoidances of CS+ and CS–.
source: Consistently, testing CS+ or CS– versus air also revealed training-induced long-lasting avoidances of CS+ and CS– (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cycloheximide (CXM) treatment abolished 1 day avoidances of CS+ and CS–.
source: Results show that such avoidances resulted from the formation of protein synthesis-dependent LTMCS+ and LTMCS– because the administration of cycloheximide (CXM), a protein synthesis inhibitor, prevented the avoidances of both CS+ and CS– after 1 day (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: It takes more than 3 hr for consolidation of mLTM to be completed.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, it takes more than 3 hr for consolidation to be completed.
evidence: This is supported by the cold-shock treatment data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LTMCS+ and LTMCS– were both extinguished by the re-exposure to either CS+ or CS– alone.
source: First, LTMCS+ and LTMCS– were both extinguished by the re-exposure to either CS+ or CS– alone (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Re-exposure to three cycles of either CS+ or CS– for 1 min with 1 min inter-trial intervals significantly reduced both LTMCS+ and LTMCS–.
source: Trained flies were re-exposed to three cycles of either CS+ or CS– for 1 min with 1 min inter-trial intervals immediately before testing. Such treatment significantly reduced both LTMCS+ and LTMCS–, as compared to those re-exposed to air, suggesting the LTMCS+ and LTMCS– are both retrievable for either one of CS+ and CS–.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LTMCS+ and LTMCS– are both retrievable by either one of CS+ and CS–.
source: Such treatment significantly reduced both LTMCS+ and LTMCS–, as compared to those re-exposed to air, suggesting the LTMCS+ and LTMCS– are both retrievable for either one of CS+ and CS–.
evidence: This is an inference based on the extinction data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LTMCS+ and LTMCS– were both abolished when the temporal interval between CS+ and CS– during training was prolonged to more than 5 min.
source: Second, LTMCS+ and LTMCS– were both abolished when the temporal interval between CS+ and CS– during training was prolonged to more than 5 min (Figure 2B), suggesting that the formation of LTMCS+ and LTMCS– depends on the contiguity of two shock-paired CS+ and CS– exposures, instead of temporally separated exposures.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The formation of LTMCS+ and LTMCS– depends on the contiguity of two shock-paired CS+ and CS– exposures.
source: Second, LTMCS+ and LTMCS– were both abolished when the temporal interval between CS+ and CS– during training was prolonged to more than 5 min (Figure 2B), suggesting that the formation of LTMCS+ and LTMCS– depends on the contiguity of two shock-paired CS+ and CS– exposures, instead of temporally separated exposures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Changing the sequence of exposure to CS+ and CS– did not affect either LTMCS+ or LTMCS–.
source: In addition, changing the sequence of exposure to CS+ and CS– did not affect either LTMCS+ or LTMCS– (Figure 2C), but training with CS+ or CS– alone failed to induce the LTMCS+ or LTMCS– (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Training with CS+ or CS– alone failed to induce the LTMCS+ or LTMCS–.
source: In addition, changing the sequence of exposure to CS+ and CS– did not affect either LTMCS+ or LTMCS– (Figure 2C), but training with CS+ or CS– alone failed to induce the LTMCS+ or LTMCS– (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Observed LTMCS+ and LTMCS– are more likely to be derived from the same memory component rather than two parallel LTMs.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that, instead of two parallel LTMs, observed LTMCS+ and LTMCS– are more likely to be derived from the same memory component.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The memory was termed as mLTM because it was observable after two separated memory curves (CS+ and CS–) merged over time.
source: Since it was observable after two separated memory curves (CS+ and CS–) merged over time, we termed it as mLTM.
evidence: This explains the naming of the merged long-term memory.

claim: In Drosophila, associative olfactory memories are mainly encoded by the DANs.
source: In Drosophila, associative olfactory memories are mainly encoded by the DANs (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Cognigni et al., 2018) through alterations of the connections between KCs and MBONs (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Cognigni et al., 2018; Dubnau and Chiang, 2013; Modi et al., 2020; Pascual and Préat, 2001; Plaçais et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Associative olfactory memories are encoded through alterations of the connections between KCs and MBONs.
source: In Drosophila, associative olfactory memories are mainly encoded by the DANs (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Cognigni et al., 2018) through alterations of the connections between KCs and MBONs (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Cognigni et al., 2018; Dubnau and Chiang, 2013; Modi et al., 2020; Pascual and Préat, 2001; Plaçais et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Blocking the release of neurotransmitter from PPL1 DANs during training impaired mLTM.
source: The results showed that blocking the release of neurotransmitter from PPL1 DANs, but not PAM DANs, during training impaired mLTM (Figure 3A), suggesting that the neuromodulation of PPL1 DANs is necessary for mLTM formation.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Blocking the release of neurotransmitter from PAM DANs during training did not impair mLTM.
source: The results showed that blocking the release of neurotransmitter from PPL1 DANs, but not PAM DANs, during training impaired mLTM (Figure 3A), suggesting that the neuromodulation of PPL1 DANs is necessary for mLTM formation.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The neuromodulation of PPL1 DANs is necessary for mLTM formation.
source: The results showed that blocking the release of neurotransmitter from PPL1 DANs, but not PAM DANs, during training impaired mLTM (Figure 3A), suggesting that the neuromodulation of PPL1 DANs is necessary for mLTM formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Inhibition of the synaptic output of all KCs through exposure to a restrictive temperature during the test abolished mLTM.
source: Inhibition of the synaptic output of all KCs (R13F02-Gal4>UAS-Shits) through exposure to a restrictive temperature during the test abolished mLTM (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: mLTM did not express when the synaptic output of αβ KCs was blocked.
source: The results showed that mLTM did not express when the synaptic output of αβ KCs was blocked, whereas inhibition of α'β' KCs and γ KCs had no significant effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of α'β' KCs had no significant effect on mLTM.
source: The results showed that mLTM did not express when the synaptic output of αβ KCs was blocked, whereas inhibition of α'β' KCs and γ KCs had no significant effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of γ KCs had no significant effect on mLTM.
source: The results showed that mLTM did not express when the synaptic output of αβ KCs was blocked, whereas inhibition of α'β' KCs and γ KCs had no significant effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The PPL1 DANs mainly integrate to the α2 and α3 compartments of the vertical α lobe of MB.
source: Prior studies on the structure of MB network have uncovered that the PPL1 DANs mainly integrate to the α2 and α3 compartments of the vertical α lobe of MB, and corresponding MBONs (α2sc and α3 clusters) have been reported to be important to aversive spaced training-induced LTM expression (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Dubnau and Chiang, 2013; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Modi et al., 2020; Pascual and Préat, 2001; Plaçais et al., 2012; Schwaerzel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Corresponding MBONs (α2sc and α3 clusters) have been reported to be important to aversive spaced training-induced LTM expression.
source: Prior studies on the structure of MB network have uncovered that the PPL1 DANs mainly integrate to the α2 and α3 compartments of the vertical α lobe of MB, and corresponding MBONs (α2sc and α3 clusters) have been reported to be important to aversive spaced training-induced LTM expression (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Dubnau and Chiang, 2013; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Modi et al., 2020; Pascual and Préat, 2001; Plaçais et al., 2012; Schwaerzel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: mLTM expression was significantly impaired by blocking α2sc MBONs.
source: Results showed that mLTM expression was significantly impaired by blocking α2sc MBONs, but not α3 MBONs (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: mLTM expression was not impaired by blocking α3 MBONs.
source: Results showed that mLTM expression was significantly impaired by blocking α2sc MBONs, but not α3 MBONs (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibiting the neural activity of α2sc MBONs using heat-inducible expression of the potassium channel Kir2.1 decreased the mLTM retrieval.
source: This conclusion was further strengthened by the result that inhibiting the neural activity of α2sc MBONs using heat-inducible expression of the potassium channel Kir2.1 decreased the mLTM retrieval (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Retrieving mLTM specifically relies on the output of α2sc MBONs.
source: Thus, these results suggest that retrieving mLTM specifically relies on the output of α2sc MBONs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figures 4A, 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 1 day after training, odor-evoked calcium responses of α2sc MBONs to CS+ and CS– were both significantly reduced when compared to responses to the novel odor.
source: Consistent with results of the behavioral assay, 1 day after training, odor-evoked calcium responses of α2sc MBONs to CS+ and CS– were both significantly reduced when compared to responses to the novel odor (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Depression of CS+ and CS– odor-evoked responses can be abolished by prolonging the temporal interval between CS+ and CS– to 10 min during training.
source: Moreover, such depression of CS+ and CS– odor-evoked responses can be abolished by prolonging the temporal interval between CS+ and CS– to 10 min during training (Figure 5C), which is consistent with the result of behavioral assay (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The depressed responses to CS+ and CS– were observed immediately after training.
source: Interestingly, when we recorded the calcium responses immediately after training, the depressed responses to CS+ and CS– were observed, suggesting the mLTM should be encoded during training (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mLTM is encoded during training.
source: Interestingly, when we recorded the calcium responses immediately after training, the depressed responses to CS+ and CS– were observed, suggesting the mLTM should be encoded during training (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The aversion to CS+ and CS– are both linked to the neural plasticity conferred by the same MBON.
source: Together, our data showed that the aversion to CS+ and CS– are both linked to the neural plasticity conferred by the same MBON.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Throughout the study, the amplitudes of long-term avoidances of CS+ and CS– are always at a similar level under various conditions.
source: First, throughout our study, the amplitudes of long-term avoidances of CS+ and CS– are always at a similar level under various conditions, including pharmacological treatment (Figure 1C), cold-shock treatment (Figure 1D), odor re-exposure (Figure 2A), paradigm alteration (Figure 2B and C), and neural circuitry manipulations (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Re-exposure to either one of CS+ and CS– alone can extinguish both CS+ avoidance and CS– avoidance.
source: Second, re-exposure to either one of CS+ and CS– alone can extinguish both CS+ avoidance and CS– avoidance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The long-term avoidances of CS+ and CS– can be recorded as the depression of odor-evoked responses in the same α2sc MBONs.
source: Third, the long-term avoidances of CS+ and CS– can be recorded as the depression of odor-evoked responses in the same α2sc MBONs (Figure 4), meanwhile, CS+ avoidance and CS– avoidance both involve the same PPL1 DANs, αβ KCs, and α2sc MBONs (Figures 3 and 4A).

claim: CS+ avoidance and CS– avoidance both involve the same PPL1 DANs, αβ KCs, and α2sc MBONs.

evidence: This is supported by the neural manipulation data shown in Figures 3 and 4A.

claim: CS+ avoidance and CS– avoidance derive from the same aversive mLTM, instead of two parallel LTMs of the same valence.
source: Thus, CS+ avoidance and CS– avoidance derive from the same aversive mLTM, instead of two parallel LTMs of the same valence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral and neural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spaced multi-trial aversive differential conditioning produces two independent LTMs of opposite valence for avoiding CS+ and approaching CS–.
source: Combining with a recent report that uses a similar third-odor test to dissect LTMs induced by multi-trial spaced training (Jacob and Waddell, 2020), we are led to conclude that spaced multi-trial aversive differential conditioning produces two independent LTMs of opposite valence for avoiding CS+ and approaching CS–, whereas single-trial aversive differential conditioning yields one mLTM that guides avoidances of both CS+ and CS–.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current study and a citation to prior work (Jacob and Waddell, 2020).

claim: Single-trial aversive differential conditioning yields one mLTM that guides avoidances of both CS+ and CS–.
source: Combining with a recent report that uses a similar third-odor test to dissect LTMs induced by multi-trial spaced training (Jacob and Waddell, 2020), we are led to conclude that spaced multi-trial aversive differential conditioning produces two independent LTMs of opposite valence for avoiding CS+ and approaching CS–, whereas single-trial aversive differential conditioning yields one mLTM that guides avoidances of both CS+ and CS–.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript.

claim: When the same dangerous situation has been experienced repeatedly, animals would remember the detailed information to guide behavior in the next similar situation.
source: When the same dangerous situation has been experienced repeatedly, animals would remember the detailed information to guide behavior in the next similar situation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of single-trial and multi-trial conditioning results.

claim: When the dangerous event has only been experienced occasionally, animals would choose to avoid all potentially dangerous cues as a more reserved survival strategy.
source: However, when the dangerous event has only been experienced occasionally, animals would choose to avoid all potentially dangerous cues as a more reserved survival strategy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of single-trial and multi-trial conditioning results.

source: Jacob and Waddell, 2020 reported that multi-trial spaced training induces depressed responses to CS+ in α2sc MBONs and α3 MBONs are required for aversive LTM to CS+, whereas the modulated responses to CS– in β'2mp MBONs and γ3, γ3β'1 MBONs appears to be responsible for the safety memory to CS–.

claim: α3 MBONs are required for aversive LTM to CS+ after multi-trial spaced training.
